clue.text: It's light even when dark

parts.note: the thing meant weighs almost nothing whatever its colour, so 'light' means not heavy, not pale, and 'dark' only seems to contradict it

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that stays light even in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' and 'dark' look like opposites of brightness; the trick is that 'light' means weightless, as in the phrase 'light as a ...', and a plume can be black and still weigh nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's plume is the proverbial example of something weighing next to nothing, whatever its colour.

clue.text: No box-office receipts for this punch-up

definitions.text: No box-office receipts for this punch-up

parts.words: No box-office receipts for this punch-up
parts.note: a brawl nobody pays to watch: costing nothing, and a bout of fisticuffs

explanation.surface: A boxing match that earned nothing at the box office.
explanation.walkthrough: The box-office suggests a professional bout; the clue means a scrap nobody charged for, so free of charge and a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A general brawl, a free-for-all, joins 'gratis' and 'brawl'.

clue.text: Unfavourable view of commercial jingle

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
a jingle is a piece of light verse

explanation.surface: A dim opinion of an advertising jingle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'view of' is a link joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse conditions or comments are hostile or harmful ones.

clue.text: Ahab's man. The brother- Marxist one ? Right

parts.note: Harpo was one of the Marx Brothers comedy team
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about which Marx brother is meant, ending in 'Right'.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Ahab hunts the whale in Melville's 'Moby-Dick'; his man throws the spear. 'The brother' sets up the Marx Brothers, Harpo being the silent one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahab's crew included spear-throwers whose job was to strike the whale, such as Queequeg.

clue.text: It sounds an uncultivated area

indicators.note: the word for uncultivated, when spoken, matches the answer

parts.note: rude in its old sense means rough, unrefined, uncultivated

explanation.surface: A patch of wild, untended land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncultivated' looks like a description of the area; it means unrefined, RUDE, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English unit of land measure, a quarter of an acre.

clue.text: He's entitled to lose one, in short

definitions.text: He's entitled to lose one, in short

parts.words: He's entitled to lose one, in short
parts.note: a man holding a hereditary title whose written abbreviation is his title word with the letters of 'one' dropped

explanation.surface: Someone with a title is told he must give one up, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: The title-holder's usual short form is BART, which is the full word with O, N and E taken away: so the abbreviation literally 'loses one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary titled commoner ranking below a baron is entitled to 'Sir' and abbreviates his rank as Bart.

clue.text: But no cause for rancour among beer-drinkers

definitions.text: But no cause for rancour among beer-drinkers

parts.words: But no cause for rancour among beer-drinkers
parts.note: resentment is the sense, but drinkers of the British ale named for its sharp taste welcome the flavour

explanation.surface: Drinkers in a pub have nothing to be resentful about.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'bitter' is a hoppy draught ale, so among beer-drinkers the sharp quality behind rancour is a welcome taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is resentful sourness of spirit, and the ale's sharp taste shares the word.

clue.text: On this side the brightest are best off

indicators.note: the letters of the word best are taken off the longer word, from its front and its end

parts.note: taken as written; that the answer also sits inside it is a coincidence, since the parse removes the letters of 'best' from front and back

explanation.surface: Those who are cleverest are better off on this side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'best off' looks like 'most comfortable'; it says remove B and EST, the letters of BEST, from BRIGHTEST.
explanation.definitionFit: The side opposite the left is the other hand's side.

clue.text: Horse in twelve that has the figure

indicators.note: the horse word is placed inside the word for twelve

parts.note: noon is twelve o'clock midday
a nag is a horse

explanation.surface: A horse among twelve has a shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twelve' is not a number of horses but the hour, NOON.
explanation.definitionFit: A nine-sided polygon is a geometric figure.

clue.text: The ankle-bone so called in hospital usually

indicators.note: the bone's name sits inside the phrase that follows, across its two words

explanation.surface: What doctors in hospital usually call the ankle-bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across hospiTAL USually; 'so called' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The talus, or astragalus, is the anatomical name for the bone at the top of the foot that forms the ankle joint.

clue.text: Slippery customer, always without money

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside: the word for always is placed around the money letter

parts.note: ever means always
L, from the Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound, so money

explanation.surface: A slippery, shifty person who is forever broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, not lacking: EVER goes round L.
explanation.definitionFit: A young eel is literally slippery, and 'customer' is a jokey word for any creature.

clue.text: Like John O'Groat's house, long needing a coat perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the words that follow 'needing' might be arranged in another way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remote house that is long overdue a coat of paint.
explanation.walkthrough: John O'Groats, at the far north-east tip of mainland Scotland, is named after Jan de Groot, whose house was said to have eight sides so that no family member sat at the head of the table. 'needing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says de Groot built an eight-sided house with eight doors to settle disputes over precedence.

clue.text: A wrinkle for the ploughman

parts.note: a line on the face seen as the groove a farmer cuts in a field, the same word serving both

explanation.surface: Advice or a tip given to a farmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrinkle' can mean a useful tip, so the surface suggests farming advice; in fact it is a crease, and the farmer's version is the trench he ploughs.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep crease in the brow and the trench left by a plough share one name.

clue.text: Traces 'for example one's return in underwear

indicators.note: the reversed pieces are placed inside the underwear word

parts.note: vests are undershirts in British usage

indicators.note: the abbreviation and the numeral are read backwards

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A clue about finding the remains of something tucked inside one's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns EG + I into IGE, which goes 'in' VESTS. A VEST in Britain is a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Vestiges are faint remaining marks or remnants of something that has gone.

clue.text: Sinking shots at this hole is a pleasure

definitions.text: Sinking shots at this hole is a pleasure

parts.words: Sinking shots at this hole is a pleasure
parts.note: golf's clubhouse bar is jokingly named after the hole beyond the last of eighteen, where drinks rather than putts go down

explanation.surface: A golfer enjoys putting at a particular hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinking shots' seems to mean holing putts; it means downing drinks at the clubhouse bar, which golfers call the hole after the eighteenth.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers call the clubhouse bar the hole that follows the eighteenth.

clue.text: Ever so jealous, Myrtle

definitions.meaning: very envious; envy is proverbially this colour, and 'ever' before the word gives a plant that keeps its leaves
a shade named after the evergreen shrub, a dark bluish tone of the leaf colour

explanation.surface: Someone called Myrtle is terribly envious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Myrtle' looks like a woman's name; it is a colour, and also an evergreen shrub, which ties to 'Ever'.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is the 'green-eyed monster', and myrtle names a dark leafy shade of that colour.

clue.text: Characteristic 'of literary Americans abroad

parts.note: alludes to Mark Twain's travel book 'The Innocents Abroad', about naive American tourists in Europe

explanation.surface: A remark about how American writers behave when they travel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain's 1869 book 'The Innocents Abroad' gives the literary Americans; the quality they display is their naivety.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's travellers were naive and guileless, and guilelessness is the quality meant.

clue.text: Journeymen for a change ?

parts.note: people making a regular trip to work, taken also as people who swap or exchange things

explanation.surface: Skilled tradesmen looking for a change of scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Journeymen' suggests qualified tradesmen; read it as men who journey daily, and 'commute' also means change or exchange.
explanation.definitionFit: People who travel daily to work, and to commute a sentence is to change it.

clue.text: Anne has style unusually novel

indicators.note: doing things unusually means in a different order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman named Anne dresses in a strikingly original fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like an adjective (new); it is the definition: Mrs Henry Wood's 1861 Victorian melodrama. 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen Wood's sensational Victorian melodrama, famous in stage versions, is a book of fiction.

clue.text: Jack's introducing Jules to the publicans

indicators.note: the sailors take the novelist into their midst, so one word is put inside the other

parts.note: a jack or jack tar is a sailor; the plural is TARS
Jules Verne, the French novelist

explanation.surface: A sailor introduces a man called Jules to the people running the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack's' reads as one man's name, but a jack is a sailor, and here it is plural; 'Jules' is the French novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Tavern keepers run inns, as publicans run pubs.

clue.text: Suitable fare for a stag party?

definitions.text: Suitable fare for a stag party?

parts.words: Suitable fare for a stag party?
parts.note: a pre-wedding men's night out seems meant, but the stag is the deer, whose meat is the dish

explanation.surface: Choosing food for a groom's all-male night out.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag party is the men's celebration before a wedding; the clue jokes on deer meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer meat is the meat of a stag.

clue.text: To a certain degree she has power

parts.note: an MA, Master of Arts, is a university degree
vis is Latin for force or power

explanation.surface: A woman who is powerful up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a certain degree' looks like 'somewhat'; it is the MA degree. 'she' defines a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, popular in mid-century Britain, so any female bearer is 'she'.

clue.text: Somewhat sour and grave in revised version

indicators.note: a revised version is a reworked form, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy, slightly sour mood in a new edition of a text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised version' rearranges GRAVE IN; 'and' is a link. 'Revised Version' is also the name of a Bible translation.
explanation.definitionFit: This acidic condiment is sour, made from fermented wine.

clue.text: Left the street when booked

definitions.meaning: in heraldry and Latin the word for the left-hand side
the street of Compton Mackenzie's 1913 novel title, '... Street', i.e. the street as named in a book

explanation.surface: Someone moved out of the road once their reservation was made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booked' suggests a reservation; it means put into a book, the novel 'Sinister Street' by Compton Mackenzie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin and heraldic term for the left-hand side is also the first word of a famous novel title naming a street.

clue.text: Bad play? No, this would be the remedy

definitions.meaning: unskilful twanging of a guitar or similar instrument

definitions.text: No, this would be the remedy
definitions.meaning: with NO in front the word becomes a quack cure

explanation.surface: Poor acting, and a suggestion of how to fix it.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is cryptic: put NO before the answer and you get NOSTRUM, a remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Idly or badly plucking strings is the strummer's style; with a prefix it gives a word for a quack cure.

clue.text: The Spanish type is three quarters gold

parts.note: three of the four compass quarters: south, east and north
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A Spanish character who is largely made of gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three-quarters' looks like 75 per cent; it is three of the four compass points. 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is Spanish for a gentleman or mister, so a typical Spanish man.

clue.text: Most boring part of railway construction

definitions.text: Most boring part of railway construction

parts.words: Most boring part of railway construction
parts.note: the dullest stage seems meant, but 'boring' means drilling through rock

explanation.surface: A complaint about the dullest stage of building a railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' means tedious on the surface but drilling here: the part of the line made by boring through a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground passage driven through a hill is made by boring.

clue.text: Bring up the most backward types here

definitions.meaning: the hindmost position, where those at the very back are found

explanation.surface: Bringing up children who are the slowest learners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' looks like 'slow to learn'; it means physically furthest back.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise a child, and the hindmost position, share the word.

clue.text: Quixotic old jade

parts.note: a jade is a worn-out horse; the one belonging to Cervantes's knight Don Quixote

explanation.surface: An idealistic, unrealistic old green gemstone or a dreamy old woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jade' suggests the stone or a scolding woman; here it is a worn-out nag, Don Quixote's horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Quixote's bony, broken-down horse in Cervantes's novel bears this name, from Spanish for 'nag before'.

clue.text: The French turn with spirit to marbles

indicators.note: the French article is turned round so its letters run the other way

parts.note: le is the French masculine word for 'the'
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: The French take a spirited turn at a game of marbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses LE to EL. The answer is the name that goes with 'marbles': the Elgin Marbles, Greek sculptures in the British Museum; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Elgin removed the Parthenon sculptures, which are known by his title as the Elgin Marbles.

clue.text: One with authority but sadly no charm

indicators.note: sadly suggests something gone wrong, so the letters of the two words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A powerful person who unfortunately lacks any charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' signals rearranging NO CHARM.
explanation.definitionFit: A king or queen is a sovereign ruler holding authority.

clue.text: It's in keeping with aloofness

definitions.meaning: something kept back for later is held in this, a stock set aside

explanation.surface: Something fitting in with a person's standoffish manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in keeping with' looks like 'consistent with'; split it: what is held 'in keeping' is a stock set aside, and 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a stock held back for later use and a reticent manner share the name.
